doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
title: Military band at Westover Field, V-disks and first jazz playing
summary: He played clarinet in the Air Transport Command band, heard Lester Young V-disks with Sergeant Baraka, and began to improvise.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah. I’d be probably a CIA guy or something. Isn’t that funny? I mean I know it was a choice you know. So I was put into the band and I was stationed in Westover Field in Springfield, Mass in a Military Air Transport Command — MATS. And I played in the band and they ran the — you know from Westover they used to go to Germany, I can’t think of the name of it, it’s still there, the Air Force base. Wiesbaden, and then there was the name of a Air Force base. And they’d go back and forth and stuff. And they even had a choice of that, did I want to go. I should have done that too. In Germany after the war would be very nice you know, I’d probably speak some German you know, probably would have grabbed some German chick for all I know. But anyhow, I played in a band and had a wonderful time. And I was there for three years, I made Sergeant, and they promised me Staff Sergeant if I re-upped and I went no, I hated the Army. But I was the band librarian and I had some decision on what we were going to play, with the First Sergeant who conducted, Sergeant Baraka was a doll. And I remember on my birthday, © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

he knew my birthday, I was invited to his house for dinner. And there I am and I didn’t drink at the time, maybe I had a beer or something, and he starts playing these V-disks, and he had Lester Young’s [scats], what is that?
Right. I’ll think of that in a moment.

Yeah, yeah, “I Got Rhythm” you know. A twelve inch V-disk. He played that for me and a couple of other things you know. It was very nice. So I had a very good time. And that’s when I started to play jazz. They had sort of a big band, and I didn’t want to play saxophone. I took I think clarinet lessons from the local symphony guy on my own and I didn’t want to play saxophone. I was going to be a legitimate clarinet player. And that’s what I played in the military band, I became the first clarinetist. There was one guy, an old guy, Rutherford, Al Rutherford, a juicer you know. He had a little red nose. He was a marvelous player. I mean you know the military band, they have a lot of transcriptions, you know, Verdi and things like that, where the clarinets play the violin parts, page after page. [scats]. You’ve got to read, and you know, they could do that. They’ve got a band sound for solos, so I would get the cadenzas and stuff you know, which was, I think, that’s when I made my first record in the sense that they had a — we used to do radio programs and somebody transcribed some of them you know, and there was one I used to have where I played a little written clarinet solo but it was sort of a jazzy kind of thing. And so then I started fooling around with improvisation and I was terrible. I played a lot of red notes you know, out of the chord.
They had a sort of, I played, they had sort of a small combo but I was interested in antique music, you know, “Muskrat Ramble” and Louis Armstrong Hot Fives and Sevens.
